sources.label: Egyptian–Israeli General Armistice Agreement, 24 Feb 1949, text (Jewish Virtual Library)
Hashemite Jordan Kingdom–Israel General Armistice Agreement, 3 Apr 1949, text (Jewish Virtual Library)
Letter dated 21 July 1949 from the UN Acting Mediator (Bunche) to the Security Council (UNISPAL)
Ralph Bunche, Nobel Peace Prize 1950, biographical article (NobelPrize.org)
Armistice Lines (1949–1967), Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs map page

claims.text: Ralph Bunche, who had succeeded the assassinated mediator, brought Israeli and Egyptian delegations to negotiate on Rhodes in January 1949.

The Egyptian–Israeli General Armistice Agreement was signed at Rhodes on 24 February 1949; it was signed for Egypt by Mahmed Seif El Dine and M. K. El Raliniany and for Israel by Walter Eytan, Yigael Yadin and Elias Sasson.

Article IV(3) of the Egyptian agreement says its provisions are 'dictated exclusively by military considerations' and valid only for the period of the armistice; Article V says the demarcation line 'is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary' and is drawn without prejudice to either party's rights in the ultimate settlement.

The Egyptian agreement required Egyptian forces in the Al Faluja pocket to withdraw beyond the Egypt–Palestine frontier under UN supervision (Annex I set the start at 0500 GMT on 26 February 1949), demilitarized the village of El Auja and its surroundings (Article VIII), and froze Egyptian forces in the Gaza–Rafah area at their positions (Article VI).

The Egyptian agreement was supervised by a seven-member Mixed Armistice Commission, three appointed by each party and chaired by the UN Truce Supervision Organization's Chief of Staff, headquartered at El Auja; it was to remain in force 'until a peaceful settlement between the Parties is achieved' (Article XII).

The Jordan–Israel agreement was signed at Rhodes on 3 April 1949, for Jordan by Colonel Ahmed Sudki El-Jundi and Lieutenant-Colonel Mohamed Maayte and for Israel by Reuven Shiloah and Lieutenant-Colonel Moshe Dayan; Article II(2) states that no provision shall prejudice the rights, claims and positions of either party in the final settlement.

Article VIII of the Jordan agreement set up a Special Committee whose agreed agenda included free access to the Holy Places and cultural institutions, use of the cemetery on the Mount of Olives, resumption of the institutions on Mount Scopus, and free movement on the Bethlehem and Latrun–Jerusalem roads.

Under Article VI of the Jordan agreement, Jordanian forces replaced Iraqi forces on the Iraqi-held front and the Wadi Ara area passed to Israel; villagers there were to keep 'full rights' of residence, property and freedom, and those who left could take movable property and be compensated for land.

Bunche's letter of 21 July 1949 called the four agreements (S/1264 Egypt, S/1296 Lebanon, S/1302 Transjordan, S/1353 Syria) 'agreements voluntarily entered into by the parties', each incorporating 'what amounts to a non-aggression pact'; the Transjordan agreement also covered the Iraqi front, making separate Iraq–Israel negotiations unnecessary.

In the same letter Bunche reported that ten members of the UN mission, including the Mediator, had died over fourteen months and about twice as many had been wounded, and concluded that with the armistices signed 'the mission of the Mediator has been fulfilled'.
The Israel–Syria agreement of 20 July 1949 completed the Rhodes armistice negotiations; Bunche received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1950, accepting it in Oslo on 10 December 1950.

Israel's Foreign Ministry describes the territory inside the 1949 armistice demarcation lines as 'about 78% of the Mandate area', notes that the agreements were meant to be interim until replaced by peace treaties, that the lines became known as the Green Line, that Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt the Gaza Strip, and that Iraq and Saudi Arabia never signed agreements with Israel.

entries.topic: Count Bernadotte's mediation: two plans, a report and an assassination (May–September 1948)

sources.label: UN press release, 17 Sep 1948: biography and activities of the Mediator (UNISPAL)
Text of Suggestions Presented by Count Bernadotte at Rhodes, 28 June 1948 (FRUS 1948, vol. V pt 2, doc. 418)
Progress Report of the UN Mediator on Palestine, 16 Sep 1948, conclusions (Jewish Virtual Library)
Progress Report of the UN Mediator, 16 Sep 1948 (Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, Institute for Palestine Studies)
Folke Bernadotte, Encyclopaedia Britannica

claims.text: Bernadotte, who as head of the Swedish Red Cross is credited with saving some 20,000 inmates of German concentration camps, was appointed UN mediator in Palestine on 20 May 1948.

The first truce he negotiated took effect on 11 June and lasted until 9 July 1948; the second, ordered by the Security Council on 15 July, was to last 'until a peaceful adjustment of the future situation of Palestine is reached'.

His suggestions presented at Rhodes on 28 June 1948 proposed that Palestine, including Transjordan, might form a union of 'one Arab and one Jewish' member; that the Negev in whole or part go to Arab territory and Western Galilee in whole or part to Jewish territory; that the City of Jerusalem be included in Arab territory with municipal autonomy for the Jewish community; and that each member control immigration within its own borders.

The June suggestions also proposed a free port at Haifa (including the refineries and terminals), a free airport at Lydda, and recognition of the right of people displaced by the conflict 'to return to their homes without restriction and to regain possession of their property'.
According to the mediator's own later report, both parties 'flatly rejected' the June suggestions.

His Progress Report, dated 16 September 1948, took as a premise that 'A Jewish State called Israel exists in Palestine' and concluded that the Negev should be Arab territory and Galilee Jewish territory, with Ramleh and Lydda in Arab territory, frontiers set by a UN technical boundaries commission, Jerusalem under 'effective United Nations control', Haifa a free port and Lydda a free airport.

The report urged that Arab refugees be allowed to return to Jewish-controlled areas 'at the earliest possible date', with adequate compensation for those choosing not to return, proposed a Palestine conciliation commission, and saw 'compelling reasons for merging the Arab territory of Palestine with the territory of Transjordan'.

Bernadotte was killed in Jerusalem on 17 September 1948 by members of the Stern Gang (Lehi); a French air force colonel serving as a UN observer, André-Pierre Sérot, was killed with him. The UN noted that the completed report reached Paris almost simultaneously with news of the assassination.
Britannica credits his work with laying groundwork for the UN Truce Supervision Organization and for UNRWA.

disputes.question: Which UN body appointed Bernadotte on 20 May 1948?

positions.view: The five permanent members of the Security Council, sitting as a committee of the General Assembly under a General Assembly resolution of 14 May 1948.
The UN Security Council named him mediator.

entries.topic: Resolution 194 in full, and how many refugees there were

sources.label: General Assembly Resolution 194 (III), 11 Dec 1948, text (Refworld/UNHCR)
UNGA Resolution 194, Economic Cooperation Foundation (Israel) issue file
Benny Morris, The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited (Cambridge UP, 2004), Appendix 1, summary
UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine, Progress Report A/1985 (Nov 1951) (Jewish Virtual Library)
Palestine Land Society, Palestinian Right of Return: compilation of the depopulated villages list

claims.text: Resolution 194 (III) was adopted at the General Assembly's 186th plenary meeting on 11 December 1948, by 35 votes to 15 with 8 abstentions.
Paragraph 2 established a Conciliation Commission of three UN member states; France, Turkey and the United States were named to it.

Paragraph 8 called for the Jerusalem area to be treated separately and placed under 'effective United Nations control', asked the Security Council to ensure its demilitarization, and instructed the Commission to propose a permanent international regime; paragraph 9 called for the 'freest possible access to Jerusalem by road, rail or air'.

Paragraph 7 called for protection of and free access to the Holy Places, including Nazareth, under 'effective United Nations supervision'; paragraph 5 urged governments to negotiate 'the final settlement of all questions outstanding between them'.

Paragraph 11, besides return and compensation, instructed the Commission to facilitate 'repatriation, resettlement and economic and social rehabilitation' of the refugees and the payment of compensation, working with the Director of UN Relief for Palestine Refugees.

Estimates of the 1948 refugee total diverged from the start: Israeli spokesmen publicly said 'about 520,000' and Israel officially held to 520,000–530,000; Arab officials from 1949 spoke of 900,000 or one million; the British estimated 810,000 in February 1949 (210,000 in Gaza, 320,000 in the West Bank, 280,000 in Lebanon, Syria and the East Bank); the UN Economic Survey Mission and UNRWA counted 726,000.

According to Benny Morris, in late 1950 Israel's Foreign Ministry director-general Walter Eytan privately called UNRWA's registration of 726,000 'meticulous' but said 'the real number was close to 800,000'.

The Conciliation Commission's November 1951 report put the value of abandoned Arab immovable property at about P£100 million (P£100,383,000), on 16,324 square kilometres of land of which 4,574 were cultivable; for its calculations it took the refugee population as approximately 900,000.

Counts of depopulated Palestinian localities differ by definition: Benny Morris (1987) identified 369 villages, Walid Khalidi (1992) 418, earlier lists 399 (al-Arif), 443 (Nijm and Muammer) and 472 (Saleh), and the Palestine Land Society, counting towns and tribal lands too, 531 localities.

disputes.question: How many Palestinians became refugees in 1948?

positions.view: About 520,000–530,000 (Israel's official public figure at the time).

About 711,000–726,000 (UN Conciliation Commission estimate cited elsewhere in this chapter; UN Economic Survey Mission and UNRWA registration of 726,000), or close to 800,000 (Eytan privately, 1950) or 810,000 (British, 1949).
900,000 or one million (Arab officials from 1949); the UNCCP used 900,000 as a working approximation for its 1951 property calculations.
369 villages (Morris 1987).
418 villages (Khalidi 1992), excluding towns and sites without permanent structures.
531 localities including towns, tribal lands and police stations (Palestine Land Society).

entries.topic: Israel's admission to the UN (May 1949) and the Jerusalem question (December 1949–January 1950)

sources.label: General Assembly Resolution 273 (III), 11 May 1949, Admission of Israel (UNISPAL)
UNGA Resolution 273, Economic Cooperation Foundation issue file
UN Ad Hoc Political Committee, 47th meeting summary record, 6 May 1949 (UNISPAL)
Federal Agency for Civic Education (Germany), "70 years ago: Knesset declares Jerusalem capital of Israel"

claims.text: Before admitting Israel, the General Assembly's Ad Hoc Political Committee on 6 May 1949 took up Israel's attitude to Resolutions 181 and 194, naming the internationalization of Jerusalem, the repatriation of refugees and the investigation of the assassination of Bernadotte and Colonel Sérot; Egypt had opposed inviting Israel's representative to explain.

Resolution 273 (III) of 11 May 1949 admitted Israel to UN membership, noting Israel's declaration that it 'unreservedly accepts the obligations of the United Nations Charter', recalling the resolutions of 29 November 1947 and 11 December 1948, and taking note of 'the declarations and explanations made by the representative of the Government of Israel' before the Ad Hoc Political Committee.
The vote on Resolution 273 was 37 in favour, 12 against and 9 abstaining.

Resolution 181 had made Jerusalem and Bethlehem a corpus separatum under UN administration; after the war Israel held West Jerusalem and Jordan held East Jerusalem including the Old City, the Temple Mount and the Western Wall, and Jews were denied access to their holy sites there.

On 9 December 1949 the General Assembly's Resolution 303 again called for international status for Jerusalem; Ben-Gurion spoke against it in the Knesset on 13 December, the Knesset moved from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem on 26 December, and on 23 January 1950 it declared Jerusalem the capital by 60 votes to 2 (the two opponents were Communists who supported international status).
According to the same source the declaration was not internationally recognized, and no state opened an embassy in West Jerusalem until 1967.

entries.topic: Barring return: the June 1948 decision, the border, and the "infiltration" years (1948–1956)

sources.label: Arthur Hertzberg, "The Turning Point?", New York Review of Books, 13 Oct 1988 (review of Morris)
Avi Shlaim, "Israel's Dirty War", London Review of Books 16:16 (1994), review of Morris, Israel's Border Wars
The Fedayeen, Jewish Virtual Library (after Mitchell Bard)

claims.text: According to Arthur Hertzberg's 1988 account of Benny Morris's research, Israel's cabinet decided on 16 June 1948 that 'there could be no return during the war', leaving the question to be reconsidered later.

Hertzberg, summarizing Morris, wrote that Jews quickly occupied abandoned houses and property from the summer of 1948 and that by the 1949 armistices Israel was unwilling and unable to allow substantial return; Morris found no formal decision to expel by the highest leaders, while commanders' authority shaped events.

Morris, in Israel's Border Wars as reviewed by Avi Shlaim, estimated that '90 per cent or more' of infiltrations in 1949–56 were motivated by economic and social concerns (returning to homes, fields, property or relatives) rather than political aims.

Between 2,700 and 5,000 infiltrators were killed in 1949–56, 'the great majority of them unarmed', according to Morris's estimate as reported by Shlaim; Israel's army, border guard and police adopted a policy of shooting suspects on sight.
In October 1953 at Qibya, Unit 101 under Ariel Sharon blew up 45 houses and killed 69 Jordanian villagers, 'the majority of them women and children', provoking international protest.

Morris divided Israel's leaders over retaliation into 'activists' led by Ben-Gurion (with Dayan and Lavon) and 'moderates' led by Moshe Sharett; Shlaim faulted him for underplaying Sharett's secret contacts with Nasser.

From the Israeli side, the Jewish Virtual Library records that on 31 August 1955 Nasser announced Egypt would dispatch 'her heroes' to Israel's borders, and describes the fedayeen as fighters trained and equipped by Egyptian intelligence to carry out attacks inside Israel, in breach of the armistice ban on paramilitary hostilities.

positions.view: Overwhelmingly economic and social: refugees returning to homes, crops and relatives; most of those killed were unarmed (Morris, via Shlaim).
A security threat that from 1955 included fedayeen organized by Egyptian intelligence, which Israel answered with retaliation (Jewish Virtual Library).

entries.topic: From abandoned property to state land: the legal chain, 1948–1953

sources.label: Michael R. Fischbach, Records of Dispossession (Columbia University Press, 2003)
Gerry Liston, "The Historical Context of the Israeli Land and Planning Law Regime", al-Majdal (BADIL)
Land Acquisition (Validation of Acts and Compensation) Law 1953, Adalah discriminatory laws database
Trachtenberg, Kedar and Shmueli, "The Development Authority and the formative years of the Israeli land regime", Journal of Israeli History 35:2 (2016)

claims.text: A Custodian of Abandoned Property was appointed on 15 July 1948; Emergency Regulations on absentees' property followed on 2 December 1948 and transferred control to a new Custodian of Absentee Property.
The Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law on 14 March 1950 as an expanded version of the 1948 regulations; it remained the main law governing refugee property for decades.

Fischbach records that in early 1949 Ben-Gurion wanted to sell a significant amount of refugee land to the Jewish National Fund, which wanted legal title transferred; his book tabulates a January 1949 sale and a 'second million' dunams bought in 1950.

A Development Authority was established in 1950; a 2016 study in the Journal of Israeli History describes it as both a major land allocator and the body that set 'the rules of the game', and finds the ban on selling 'national lands' strictly kept in rural areas but not in urban ones.

According to a BADIL analysis, the 1950 law let the Custodian transfer absentee land to the Development Authority, which could pass it to the JNF; nearly 2.4 million dunams were transferred, 'more than trebling the JNF's holdings as of 1941', and by 1951 the government (with the JNF) held 92% of land within the state.

The Land Acquisition (Validation of Acts and Compensation) Law of 1953 retroactively validated land seizures made during and after the war on grounds of security and development; the Finance Minister said its purpose was to 'instill legality in some acts undertaken during and following the war'.

Adalah states that 1.2–1.3 million dunams were expropriated from Arab owners under the 1953 law, from 349 towns and villages, and that Arab ownership has fallen to 3–3.5% of land compared with 48% in 1948 (Adalah's figures).

disputes.question: When were the absentee property regulations issued?

positions.view: 2 December 1948 (Fischbach, from Israeli sources).
A US document cited by Fischbach refers to an "Israeli ordinance of December 12, 1948".

entries.topic: Military government over Arab citizens, and the citizens who stayed (1948–1950s)

sources.label: Alina Korn, "In the Name of Security", Adalah Review vol. 4
Akevot Institute, the Toledano letter on military rule (archival document, 1967)
Jewish and non-Jewish population of Israel/Palestine (Jewish Virtual Library, after Israel CBS)
Democratic List of Nazareth, Israel Democracy Institute

claims.text: Israel's population at the end of 1948 is given as 716,700 Jews and 156,000 non-Jews; by 1950 it was 1,203,000 Jews and 167,100 non-Jews (Israel Central Bureau of Statistics figures as compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library).
In the first Knesset election in 1949 the Democratic List of Nazareth, an Arab party described as a satellite list of Mapai, won 7,387 votes (1.7%) and 2 seats.
The military government was officially established in October 1948 with five military governors; after the fighting ended it was 'neither cancelled nor was it legally regularized'.

Its main legal tools were the British Defence (Emergency) Regulations of 1945, absorbed into Israeli law by Article 11 of the Law and Administration Ordinance of 1948, above all Regulation 125, which let the military commander declare 'any area or location a closed area', together with the Emergency Regulations (Security Zones) of 1949.

According to Korn, the travel-permit requirement had no legal foundation for its first 18 months, until January 1950; in 1958 only one in three Arabs in military-government areas held a travel permit.

Korn reports that between 1948 and 1967 about a third of all convictions of Arab citizens were for violations of the Defence Regulations, about 95% of them administrative offences such as lacking a permit; in 1955, 2,714 of the 2,888 people convicted under the regulations were Arab.

The government justified the regime on security grounds; the Rattner Commission of February 1956 concluded it should not end until 'true peace' existed, while Korn argues its main purposes were controlling Arab residents' movement and preventing access to confiscated land.
The Knesset eased the regime in 1962 and rejected abolition bills in 1963; it voted on 8 November 1966 to end the military government, which was abolished on 1 December 1966.

Six months after abolition, the Prime Minister's adviser on Arab affairs, Shmuel Toledano, wrote to Levi Eshkol on 4 April 1967 that 'in practice, hardly any restrictions have been loosened', since closed areas and travel passes remained.

disputes.question: What was the military government for?

positions.view: Security: the Rattner Commission (1956) judged it necessary until true peace.
Control of movement and of access to confiscated land (Korn).

entries.topic: The Law of Return (1950) and the Nationality Law (1952)

sources.label: Law of Return 5710-1950, text with 1970 amendment (My Jewish Learning)
Law of Return 1950 with amendments, Adalah discriminatory laws database (statutory text)
"Law of Return", Encyclopaedia Judaica (2nd ed.) and Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa, via Encyclopedia.com
Nationality Law 5712-1952, text (Refworld)
Anis F. Kassim, "The Israeli Law of Return" (AARDI / Institute for Palestine Studies, 2021)

claims.text: Section 1 of the Law of Return states: 'Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh.' Section 2 requires an oleh's visa for every Jew who wishes to settle, unless the minister finds the applicant is acting against the Jewish people or likely to endanger public health or state security; section 4 deems Jews already in the country, or born there, to have come as olim.
The law was signed by Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, Minister of Immigration Moshe Shapira and Yosef Sprinzak as Acting President and Knesset Chairman, and is dated 20 Tammuz 5710 (5 July 1950).

Presenting the bill, Ben-Gurion said the right 'is inherent in every Jew by virtue of his being a Jew' and that 'This right preceded the State of Israel'; the Encyclopaedia Judaica links the law to the Basel Program (1897), Article 6 of the Mandate (1922) and the Declaration of Independence.

A 1954 amendment (23 August 1954) added an exclusion for a person 'with a criminal past, likely to endanger public welfare'; the 1970 amendment extended rights to a Jew's child, grandchild and spouses and defined a Jew as one 'born of a Jewish mother or has become converted to Judaism and who is not a member of another religion'.

The Nationality Law of 1952 provided that every oleh under the Law of Return becomes a national 'by return', while a former Palestinian citizen could become a national 'by residence' only if registered as an inhabitant on 1 March 1952, an inhabitant on the day the law took effect, and continuously in Israel (or entered legally) from the state's establishment; it took effect on 14 July 1952 and repealed the Palestinian Citizenship Orders retroactively to the establishment of the state.

The Palestinian jurist Anis Kassim argues the Law of Return amounts to 'legally-authorized racial discrimination', that 'an indigenous Palestinian has no such inherent right even if he used to live on the land', and that Palestinians who stayed were left stateless for about thirty years.

Within Jewish debate, the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East notes that some Orthodox leaders wanted a narrower definition of 'Jew', Reform and Conservative movements opposed that, and some non-Zionists called for repeal as discriminatory.

disputes.question: On what date did the Knesset pass the Law of Return?

positions.view: 5 July 1950 (20 Tammuz 5710), as dated in the law itself and in the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East; Kassim says adopted 5 July after bills were submitted 3 July.
3 July 1950, the anniversary of Herzl's death (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

disputes.question: Is the Law of Return a law of repatriation or of discrimination?

positions.view: A right of return inherent in being Jewish, preceding the state (Ben-Gurion; Encyclopaedia Judaica).
Legally authorized discrimination that grants Jews from anywhere what it denies to Palestinians who lived on the land (Kassim).

entries.topic: The mass immigration of 1948–1952: numbers, camps and austerity

sources.label: Independent Israel: Aliyah and Absorption (Jewish Agency for Israel, historical archive)
Immigrants to Israel, 1948–1952 (Jewish Virtual Library, from Israel State Archives)
"When Israelis Stood in Line for Rations", National Library of Israel blog

claims.text: According to the Jewish Agency, 203,000 Jews from 42 countries arrived in Israel's first year, and 684,201 immigrants arrived between May 1948 and the end of 1951, 'more than the entire Jewish population when independence was declared'.

The first arrivals were former illegal immigrants held by the British in Cyprus and Holocaust survivors from displaced-persons camps in Germany, Austria and Italy; whole communities followed, including 121,512 of Iraq's 130,000 Jews, 37,000-plus of Bulgaria's 45,000, 30,500 of Libya's 35,000 and nearly all of Yemen's 45,000.

A table from the Israel State Archives gives 738,891 immigrants from 1948 to the end of 1952: 377,251 from Muslim countries (including Iraq 124,226, Yemen and Aden 48,375, Tunisia–Morocco–Algeria 52,584, Turkey 35,025, Syria and Lebanon 34,608, Libya 32,129, Iran 25,593, Egypt 17,114) and 307,082 from Communist states (including Romania 121,537 and Poland 106,751).

By May 1950, of 393,197 arrivals since May 1948, 112,015 remained in immigrant camps and temporary housing; transitional camps (ma'abarot), where newcomers could work, were introduced in 1950, and by May 1952 there were 113 of them housing 250,000 people.
Immigration fell after the 1951 peak: 51,463 immigrants arrived in 1952–1954.

The austerity regime (tzena) rationed food by coupon (oil, sugar, margarine, rice; meat about weekly, fish about twice a month), furniture and clothing; a black market grew, merchants struck in summer 1950, the anti-rationing General Zionists won 20 Knesset seats in 1951, a New Economic Policy began easing in 1952, and rationing was officially abolished in 1959.

entries.topic: The Jews of the Arab world after 1948: violence, law and departure

sources.label: Victims of the riots in Oujda and Jérada, June 1948 (JewishGen, Jeff Malka Sephardic Collection)
Jews of Egypt (Jewish Virtual Library, citing Sachar and 1956 wire reports)
Philip Mendes, "Forgotten Jewish refugees demand recognition", Eureka Street, Sept 2010

claims.text: On 7–8 June 1948, three weeks after Israel's founding, riots against Jews in Oujda and Jérada in Morocco killed 5 Jews in Oujda and 38 people in Jérada, with more than a hundred wounded; the riots are linked to young Jews crossing the border near Oujda en route to France and Israel.

Egypt's Jewish population was about 75,000 in 1948; bombs set off in the Jewish quarter of Cairo between June and November 1948 killed more than 70 Jews and wounded nearly 200 (Howard Sachar, as cited by the Jewish Virtual Library).

After the 1956 Sinai campaign the Egyptian government expelled almost 25,000 Jews and confiscated their property, about 1,000 more were detained, and a proclamation read in mosques on 23 November 1956 declared 'all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state' (per contemporary AP and New York World-Telegram reports cited by the Jewish Virtual Library).

Philip Mendes counts nearly one million Jews (Mizrahim) who left Arab countries in the decade or so after 1947–48, most going to Israel, and finds the exodus best explained as 'a complex combination of push and pull factors': harassment, discrimination and in Iraq expulsion on one side, the pull of Zionism and of life in Israel on the other.

Mendes notes that many Egyptian Jews appear to have left for economic reasons rather than specific persecution, and characterizes the two partisan narratives: one that attributes the exodus almost solely to Arab violence, the other to 'a malicious Zionist conspiracy'.

disputes.question: Why did the Jews of the Arab world leave?

positions.view: Almost solely Arab violence or threats of violence (the narrative Mendes attributes to Zionist/Israeli accounts).
Zionist activity and agitation (the narrative Mendes attributes to Arab/anti-Zionist accounts).
A combination varying by country: persecution and expulsion pushed, Zionism pulled (Mendes).

entries.topic: Who would govern Arab Palestine: the All-Palestine Government, Jericho and Jordan's annexation (1948–1951)

sources.label: Avi Shlaim, "The Rise and Fall of the All-Palestine Government in Gaza", Journal of Palestine Studies 20:1 (1990)
Jordan: A Country Study (Library of Congress Federal Research Division)
Martin Kramer, "The ghost of annexation past", Washington Institute, June 2020
British Cabinet conclusions, 25 April 1950 (CAB 128/17), via Jewish Virtual Library

claims.text: The Arab League set up a temporary civil administration for Palestine on 8 July 1948 and in September agreed to an Arab government seated in Gaza, announced on 20 September; on 22 September an Arab Higher Committee communiqué declared Palestine independent under the All-Palestine Government headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi.

A Palestinian National Council met in Gaza on 30 September 1948 under Hajj Amin al-Husayni, adopted a provisional constitution and declared independence over all of Palestine; Egypt recognized the government first, then Iraq, then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia in mid-October, while King Abdullah refused.

Shlaim argues Egypt sponsored the government as a 'focal point of opposition to Abdullah' to frustrate his plan to join Arab Palestine to Transjordan, and calls it 'a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states, with Egypt at their head'; after Israel's October 1948 offensive its ministers were moved to Cairo, and Nasser closed its offices in 1959.

On the same day, 30 September 1948, a rival congress in Amman pledged loyalty to Abdullah; the Jericho Congress of 1 December 1948 proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king.

Abdullah took the title of king in December 1948 and in April 1949 ordered the country called the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan; elections on both banks were held in April 1950, after which he formally annexed the West Bank. About 500,000 Palestinian Arabs took refuge in Transjordan or the West Bank, which had about 500,000 indigenous residents; Transjordan's prewar population was about 340,000.
On 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament resolved in favour of 'complete unity between the two banks of the Jordan, the eastern and western, and their union in one single state'.
Britain's cabinet on 25 April 1950 agreed to recognize the union of Arab Palestine and Jordan together with the State of Israel.

The Library of Congress study says the annexation was recognized only by Britain and Pakistan and was condemned within the Arab League as advancing Hashemite dynastic ambitions; Kramer notes Israelis customarily hold that only Britain, or Britain and Pakistan, recognized it.

On 20 July 1951 Abdullah was assassinated entering al-Aqsa Mosque for Friday prayers, with his grandson Hussein at his side; the assassin, a Palestinian, was reportedly hired by relatives of Hajj Amin al-Husayni.

disputes.question: Which states recognized Jordan's annexation of the West Bank?

positions.view: Britain and Pakistan only (Library of Congress country study; one customary Israeli account per Kramer).
Britain only (the other customary Israeli account per Kramer).

entries.topic: Paying for the new state: US loans and grants, Israel Bonds and German reparations (1949–1953)

sources.label: Total US foreign aid to Israel, 1949–present (Jewish Virtual Library, from CRS, Jeremy Sharp)
State of Israel Bonds (Jewish Virtual Library)
German Holocaust reparations (Jewish Virtual Library, citing Israel MFA 1953 documents and Encyclopaedia Judaica)
"The Reparations Agreement of 1952 and the response in Israel", National Library of Israel blog

claims.text: US assistance to Israel, per the Congressional Research Service table compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library (millions of dollars): 1949, 100.0 (Export-Import Bank and other); 1950, 0; 1951, 35.1; 1952, 86.4; 1953, 73.6; 1954, 74.7; 1955, 52.7; 1956, 50.8; 1957, 40.9; 1958, 85.4; 1959, 53.3, the last including the first military loan of 0.4.

Ben-Gurion conceived an overseas bond issue in 1950 amid economic crisis and mass immigration, convened American Jewish leaders at the King David Hotel in September 1950, and launched sales in the United States the following spring with a rally at Madison Square Garden; the 1951 Independence Issue paid 3.5 percent and first-year sales topped $52 million.

Within six years bond sales accounted for 35% of Israel's special development budget, financing projects including the National Water Carrier, the Dead Sea Works, power plants, ports and immigrant towns.

On 12 March 1951 Moshe Sharett claimed $1.5 billion from Germany, calculated as the cost of absorbing 500,000 Nazi victims at $3,000 each; on 9 January 1952 the Knesset voted 61–50 to negotiate directly with West Germany while thousands protested outside and police used tear gas.
Menachem Begin led the opposition, speaking at mass demonstrations in spring 1952; opponents called the payments 'blood money' from the 'land of the murderers'.

The agreement was signed in Luxembourg on 10 September 1952 by Sharett, Nahum Goldmann and Konrad Adenauer and took effect on 21 March 1953; payments ran in annual instalments from 1 April 1953 to 31 March 1966, 30% for crude oil bought in Britain and 70% for German goods, and made up 12–14% of Israel's annual imports over the decade.

The value of the agreement is given as $845 million, of which $100 million went to the Claims Conference (Jewish Virtual Library), or as goods and services worth 3.5 billion marks over 12 years plus 450 million marks more (National Library of Israel).

disputes.question: How large was the 1952 reparations agreement, and over what period?

positions.view: $845 million in total, $100 million of it for the Claims Conference, paid over 14 years (1953–1966).
Goods and services valued at 3.5 billion marks over 12 years, plus 450 million marks.

sources.label: Michael Dickerman, "The Israeli Constitutional Decision of 1950", The Reconstructionist 71:2 (2007), via Berman Jewish Policy Archive

claims.text: The Declaration of Independence promised a constitution 'adopted by the Elected Constituent Assembly not later than the 1st October 1948'.
The Constituent Assembly elected in January 1949 convened on 14 February 1949 and two days later renamed itself the Knesset.

Ben-Gurion opposed a written constitution, partly to avoid judicial limits on government and partly fearing that a fight over religion would deepen the religious–secular divide during the conflict; religious parties insisted on religious courts' exclusive authority over personal status.

On 13 June 1950, after nine debates, the Knesset adopted the Harari Resolution (moved by Yizhar Harari of the Progressive Party): the constitution 'will be made up of chapters, each of which will constitute a separate basic law', and 'all the chapters together will constitute the constitution of the state'.
